title: American Summers Are Getting Dangerously Hotter. If You Have South Asian Genes, Your Heart Is Already at Higher Risk.
excerpt: A new study projects a 34 per cent rise in heat-related cardiovascular disease by 2050 — driven by warming and ageing demographics. For a community with elevated baseline cardiac risk, the overlap is alarming.
body:
Meteorological summer began on June 1 across the United States, and for the first time in decades, public health officials are treating the season less like a weather event and more like a cardiovascular emergency.

A sweeping analysis released this week by Climate Central found that 97 per cent of 243 US cities have experienced warmer summers since 1970, with an average increase of 2.6 degrees Fahrenheit. Reno, Nevada, leads the country with 68 additional hotter-than-normal summer days compared to the early 1970s — an 11.3-degree jump. Houston (58 extra days), Las Vegas (6.2 degrees warmer), and Salt Lake City (6.0 degrees warmer) round out the most affected metros.

But the heat itself is only half the story. A parallel study published in a cardiovascular epidemiology journal projects that rising temperatures could drive a 34 per cent increase in heat-related cardiovascular disease by 2050 — even before accounting for climate change. That 34 per cent figure comes from demographic shifts alone: the growing number of older adults in the population. Layer in the warming trend, and the outlook becomes considerably grimmer.

Why the Pacific Northwest Is a Surprise Hotspot

One of the study's most counterintuitive findings is that the Pacific Northwest currently has the highest rates of heat-related heart disease in the country. The reason is infrastructure, not latitude. Cities such as Portland and Seattle historically built few buildings with air conditioning, and their emergency-response systems were designed for mild summers. When temperatures spike, residents and healthcare systems are less prepared than those in Phoenix or Dallas.

Going forward, however, the greatest increases are projected for the South — where high baseline cardiovascular disease rates, significant warming, and lower-income communities with limited healthcare access create a dangerous convergence.

The South Asian Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, these numbers carry an additional layer of urgency. The MASALA study — the largest longitudinal study of South Asian cardiovascular health in the United States — has consistently found that South Asian adults develop prediabetes at nearly double the rate of other ethnic groups and show elevated markers of subclinical atherosclerosis even when traditional risk factors appear normal.

A separate analysis published earlier this year found that 30 per cent of South Asian adults in the US have prediabetes by age 45, despite reporting some of the healthiest diets of any ethnic group. The metabolic paradox — lean body mass concealing visceral fat, insulin resistance masked by normal BMI — means that heat stress lands on a cardiovascular system already running closer to its limits.

When the body overheats, it diverts blood flow to the skin for cooling, raising heart rate and blood pressure. In individuals with subclinical cardiac strain, this thermoregulatory burden can trigger arrhythmias, ischaemic events, and in extreme cases, sudden cardiac arrest.

What Families Can Do

Cardiologists working with South Asian populations recommend a summer-specific checklist:

Monitor medications. Diuretics and beta-blockers — commonly prescribed for hypertension — can impair the body's ability to cool itself. If you or a parent takes either, discuss summer dosing with a physician.

Track the heat index, not just the temperature. Humidity amplifies cardiac stress. The National Weather Service heat index combines both into a single "feels like" number. When it exceeds 105°F, even healthy adults face elevated risk.

Prioritise nighttime cooling. A Texas-based study found that nighttime temperatures that fail to drop below 75°F prevent the body from recovering from daytime heat stress. If your home does not have reliable air conditioning, public cooling centres — available in most US counties — can be life-saving for elderly family members.

Check on parents in India. The current Indian heatwave has killed more than 2,200 people, the country's deadliest in 28 years. If you have ageing family members in northern or central India, daily wellness calls during the afternoon peak (2-5 PM IST) are not excessive — they are necessary.

The Bigger Picture

Climate researchers are increasingly framing summer heat as a chronic public health threat rather than an acute weather event. For a diaspora community spread across the Sun Belt — Houston, Dallas, Phoenix, Atlanta — and simultaneously connected to families in a warming subcontinent, this is a dual exposure that no other demographic quite shares.

The data does not say panic. It says plan. Get baseline cardiac markers checked. Keep medications current. Ensure cooling access for the oldest members of your household, here and back home. Summer is no longer just a season. For South Asians, it is now a cardiovascular risk factor.

Sources: Climate Central 2026 summer warming analysis; cardiovascular heat projection study (2050 model); MASALA study (Northwestern University); India Meteorological Department heatwave data 2026.
